reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a BNB front-running bot and instructs viewers to deploy and fund it through MetaMask and PancakeSwap. It claims that a 0.5 BNB investment can return 0.24 BNB in about three minutes, while recommending minimum funding and suggesting that larger funding can produce larger profits. The stated risk warning does not remove the video's solicitation of rapid crypto profits.

citations.quote: We are going to be coding our very own front runner bot contract to run on PancakeSwap on the Binance Smart Chain.

this will allow our transaction to be processed first and then we will also process a sell order within the same block so essentially the victim transaction gets sandwiched between hours and we make a small profit off the slippage difference in the transaction
we're going to click deploy
we are going to need to fund our contract with BNB
the more you put in, the larger the transaction, you'll be able to front run, and the more profit you'll be able to make

opening.argument: Judge the presentation as a conditional trading demonstration, not a promise of returns. The speaker explicitly tells viewers that investing more is their choice and at their own risk because the bot may target a honeypot. He also says he limits the amount he uses. The description accounts for gas and possible burn fees, costs that qualify the headline profit claim. Those warnings do not prove the contract works, but they make an unconditional-profit reading too strong.

citations.quote: if you want to go ahead and invest more, you're more than welcome to, however that's at your own risk – you never know what type of contract the bot will snipe. It could be a honeypot
I always play it safe and half a BNB to one BNB.
I got messages from people who didn't fund enough to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited deployment and funding instructions establish what the tutorial asks viewers to do, but they do not establish that a return is guaranteed. Nor does the description present funding as costless: it warns about gas and burn fees. The speaker's own risk warning specifically identifies uncertainty about which contract the bot might target.

citations.quote: I got messages from people who didn't fund enough to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.
however that's at your own risk – you never know what type of contract the bot will snipe

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A risk warning does not undo the instruction to fund the contract or the pitch that adding more money can produce more profit. The speaker also presents a rapid return on the amount he says he invested. Those are concrete inducements to commit BNB, regardless of whether he promises every viewer the same result.

opening.argument: The core of this video is a walkthrough of a Solidity workflow. The speaker explains pending transactions and gas ordering, then takes viewers through creating a contract file and selecting the matching compiler version in Remix. Deploying and funding are shown as subsequent steps in that demonstration. A technical tutorial can describe a proposed profit mechanism without independently proving that it succeeds; the cited steps alone establish instruction, not a verified return.

citations.quote: look for transactions that are pending to be made within a block and that is going to allow us to inject our transaction with a higher gas fee
Click that, and that will help us... ...create a new file. So this will be our contract.
under Compiler, we are going to select... our version of Solidity, which matches up over here... which is 0.6 point 6
we're going to click deploy
we are going to need to fund our contract with BNB

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening cites a description of transaction ordering and two workflow steps. Those passages support calling the video an instruction, but do not by themselves verify that the contract generated profits. The broader walkthrough includes file creation and compilation, so the deploy-and-fund steps need to be read in their technical-demonstration context.

citations.quote: Click that, and that will help us... ...create a new file. So this will be our contract.
we are going to click the Solidity Compiler.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The technical format is precisely how the viewer is led to put BNB into the contract. The speaker supplies contract text, directs deployment and funding, and reports a quick profit from the purported run. Whether that result is independently verified is not the point: the video presents it as a reason to follow the funded workflow.

we are going to need to fund our contract with BNB
That was about 3 minutes Off of 0.5 BNB Investment We've already sniped 0.24

opening.argument: The observed funding is described as capital for a contract the viewer deploys and uses for trading, not as a payment for access to a seller's promised payout. The speaker identifies Remix as the place to develop and launch the contract and says the viewer can choose how much BNB to fund it with. He also says the action can pull the initially entered BNB back. None of those statements independently verifies custody or withdrawals, but the cited workflow does not identify a required transfer to a named third-party recipient or a guaranteed payout schedule.

citations.quote: Remix is an application that is developed to allow us to develop, compile, launch, and transact with smart contracts on the Binance Smart Chain that are coded in the Solidity language.
You can fund the contract with however much BNB you want to try to snipe the mempool with
it will pull the BNB that you entered initially back towards you

rebuttal.rebuttal: Funding a deployed contract is not, on its own, evidence that BNB goes to the presenter; the speaker describes funding it to pursue trades. The opening's profit interpretation also goes beyond what its cited deploy and fund instructions prove. A claim about a demonstrated return should be assessed as a claim, not treated as independent proof of an actual payout.

citations.quote: we are going to need to fund our contract with BNB... ...to be able to snipe liquidity pools.
That was about 3 minutes Off of 0.5 BNB Investment We've already sniped 0.24

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A named third-party recipient or fixed payout schedule is not necessary to recognize the solicitation. The speaker directs viewers to fund a supplied contract, says more capital can mean more profit, and claims a fast return. The assertion that the initial BNB can be pulled back is itself part of the pitch, not independent evidence that viewers can recover it.
